theme: Major challenges of the Indian economy
question: Explain the causes and consequences of the current account deficit and a falling rupee. Suggest measures to correct an unfavourable balance of payments.
why: Major challenges (inflation, CAD, BoP, falling rupee, NPAs, black money) are listed together in the first Paper IV syllabus item; each is a factual, repeatable question.
intro: The current account records trade in goods and services, income and transfers. A deficit (imports and payments above exports and receipts) must be financed by capital inflows. Persistent deficits put pressure on the exchange rate.

body.h: Causes of CAD and rupee depreciation
pts: High oil and gold imports, electronics dependence, slower exports, global dollar strength and capital outflows by foreign investors.
Inflation differentials and high fiscal deficit.
Costlier imports and imported inflation, higher external debt servicing, volatility in markets and risk to growth; but weaker rupee helps exporters.

Export promotion and diversification, FTAs, reducing oil imports through ethanol blending, renewables and EVs, import substitution through PLI, attracting FDI and stable portfolio flows, building forex reserves and RBI's market intervention, remittances and services exports.
NPAs: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, recapitalisation and asset reconstruction; black money: demonetisation, GST, Benami Act, FEMA enforcement.

conclusion: A moderate CAD is manageable for a growing economy; the aim is to keep it financed by stable long-term flows. Structural export competitiveness is the lasting solution.

theme: Public debt, FDI/FII and external resources
question: Distinguish between FDI and FII. Discuss the desirability and consequences of utilising different sources of external finance for India's development.
why: The syllabus lists sources of resources: public debt, external debt from multilateral agencies, FII and FDI with 'desirability and consequences' — a direct question pattern.
intro: External resources supplement domestic savings. They come as foreign direct investment (long-term, with control), foreign portfolio investment (short-term securities) and external debt from lenders such as the World Bank, ADB and bilateral partners.

pts: FDI: lasting interest and management control, brings technology and jobs, stable, difficult to withdraw.
FPI/FII: investment in stocks and bonds, liquid, volatile, can reverse quickly and trigger market and rupee shocks.
Concessional multilateral loans (World Bank, ADB, NDB) fund infrastructure and social projects; commercial borrowings are costlier and exchange-risky.
India's external debt is moderate relative to GDP, with a large share long-term.
Benefits: capital, technology, exports and competition; risks: dependence, repatriation of profits, exposure to global cycles and conditionalities.
Policy: prefer FDI and equity over debt, FDI liberalisation through the automatic route, caps on short-term external borrowing, adequate reserves.

conclusion: External finance should supplement, not substitute, domestic resources. A mix tilted towards stable FDI and long-term concessional loans reduces risk.

theme: Agriculture in Andhra Pradesh: cropping pattern, horticulture, fisheries and dairying
question: Discuss the changing cropping pattern in Andhra Pradesh and the role of horticulture, fisheries and dairying in diversifying the agricultural economy.
why: AP agriculture (8.x) is a named syllabus item; changing cropping pattern, horticulture, fisheries and dairy are explicitly listed.
intro: Andhra Pradesh has shifted from cereals towards commercial crops, horticulture and aquaculture. It is among India's leading producers of rice, chilli, mango, oil palm, shrimp and fish.

pts: Decline in area under jowar, millets and pulses in many districts; expansion of paddy in deltas, cotton and chilli in Guntur–Krishna, groundnut in Rayalaseema, tobacco in Prakasam; shift towards oil palm, maize and horticulture.
Horticulture: mango, banana, citrus, sweet orange, coconut and spices; Rayalaseema's horticulture hubs.
Fisheries and aquaculture: shrimp and fish exports from the Godavari-Krishna delta; Visakhapatnam and Kakinada ports; fisheries harbours.
Dairy and poultry: milk production, cooperative dairies such as Vijaya and the poultry belt of Godavari districts.
Price volatility, disease and export standards, disaster risk, water stress; need cold chains, processing, FPOs and crop-neutral income support.

conclusion: Diversification has raised farm incomes and exports. A value-chain approach will make the shift sustainable.

theme: Infrastructure: transport, energy, urban and PPP
question: Public-private partnership has been widely used for infrastructure in India. Discuss its advantages, problems and the pricing of public utilities.
why: Infrastructure in India (item 11) lists PPP, pricing of public utilities and environmental impacts explicitly; PPP is a perennial analytic question.
intro: India needs large investment in roads, ports, airports, railways, energy and urban services. Government resources are limited, so PPP models are used to bring private capital and efficiency.

pts: BOT (toll or annuity), DBFOT, HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model) in highways, concessions in ports and airports (Hyderabad, Delhi), VGF support, InvITs and the National Monetisation Pipeline.
Mobilises private funds and expertise, faster construction, risk-sharing, better maintenance.
Land acquisition delays, over-optimistic traffic projections, renegotiation and disputes, bank stress after overleveraged projects, tariff controversies, weak regulation.
Public utilities need cost-reflective yet affordable tariffs through independent regulators; cross-subsidies; subsidy transparency.
Environmental impact assessment and rehabilitation should be built into project design.

conclusion: PPP works when risks are shared fairly and contracts are transparent. Sound regulation and project preparation protect both public interest and private investors.

theme: Infrastructure in Andhra Pradesh: ports, energy and ICT
question: Discuss the ongoing infrastructure projects of Andhra Pradesh in transport, energy and ICT, and the bottlenecks in their implementation.
why: AP infrastructure (item 12) lists transport, energy, ICT, bottlenecks, policy and ongoing projects; projects can change, but the structure of the answer is stable.
intro: With a long coastline, major ports and corridors, Andhra Pradesh is positioned as a logistics and industrial gateway. Infrastructure determines whether it can attract investment.

pts: Ports: Visakhapatnam, Gangavaram, Krishnapatnam, Kakinada; proposed Ramayapatnam, Machilipatnam and Bhavanapadu.

Visakhapatnam–Chennai Industrial Corridor, national highways and the Amaravati outer ring road, freight corridors, airports at Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Tirupati, Rajahmundry and the proposed greenfield Bhogapuram airport.
Thermal plants at Krishnapatnam and Sri Damodaram Sanjeevaiah, solar parks (Kurnool, Ananthapuramu), wind in Rayalaseema, pumped storage proposals and green hydrogen/ammonia hubs.
Fibre-to-home network (AP Fibernet), IT parks at Visakhapatnam, e-governance such as Grama Sachivalayam services.
Funding gaps and debt, land acquisition, slow approvals and power-purchase dues, last-mile and rural connectivity gaps.

conclusion: Infrastructure is the state's growth platform. Timely execution and PPP support are needed to turn its location advantage into industrial growth.

question: What is energy security? Discuss India's energy mix and the policy measures to achieve energy security and clean energy transition.
why: Energy needs, resources, policy and security are listed in the 2026 syllabus; energy is the second-most asked theme (24 questions).
intro: Energy security is the uninterrupted availability of energy at affordable prices and with acceptable environmental impact. India imports about four-fifths of its oil and a large part of its gas, which makes security a strategic concern.

pts: Coal remains the main source of electricity; oil and gas for transport and industry; growing renewables (solar, wind, small hydro, biomass) and nuclear.
Per capita energy use is low; demand will rise with growth.
Renewable targets (500 GW non-fossil by 2030), National Solar Mission, wind-solar hybrid policy, green hydrogen mission, ethanol blending, PM-KUSUM and Surya Ghar rooftops.
Energy efficiency: PAT scheme, BEE star labelling, UJALA LED programme, Energy Conservation Act.
Diversification: strategic petroleum reserves, overseas assets, international solar alliance, cross-border grids, nuclear expansion.
Import dependence, discom finances, storage and transmission gaps, price volatility and just-transition concerns for coal regions.

conclusion: Energy security today means a diversified and cleaner mix with efficient use. Domestic renewables and storage are the surest hedge against import risk.

theme: Environment Impact Assessment and environmental legislation
question: Explain the process of Environment Impact Assessment in India and evaluate its effectiveness. Mention the main environmental laws that govern it.
why: EIA is a named syllabus item in two places (item 5 and environmental legislation in item 6); asked repeatedly in the compilation.
intro: EIA is a systematic process to predict the environmental effects of a project before approval so that damage can be avoided or minimised. In India it is governed by the EIA Notification 2006 issued under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986.

pts: Screening (Category A and B projects), scoping with terms of reference, baseline data and impact prediction, public consultation and hearing, appraisal by expert committees, grant of environmental clearance with conditions, and monitoring.

Environment (Protection) Act 1986, Air and Water Acts, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Wildlife Protection Act 1972, Biological Diversity Act 2002, National Green Tribunal Act 2010, CRZ and international conventions (Montreal, Kyoto, CITES, UNFCCC).
Strengths: public participation, conditions on projects, NGT review.
Weaknesses: poor quality of reports by consultants, weak monitoring, ex-post clearances, exemptions in draft notifications, limited cumulative impact assessment.
Independent accredited assessors, strong public hearings, digital compliance monitoring, strategic and cumulative assessment.

conclusion: EIA balances development and conservation only if it is credible. Independent assessment and strict follow-up make it effective.

theme: Water resources, watershed management and soil conservation
question: Discuss the importance of watershed management for water and soil conservation in India with special reference to the drought-prone areas of Andhra Pradesh.
why: Water resources, watershed management, soil reclamation, coastal and soil erosion are separate syllabus lines; Rayalaseema gives the AP context.
intro: A watershed is the area from which rainfall drains to a common point. Managing it conserves soil and water, recharges groundwater and supports rain-fed agriculture, which covers over half of India's cropped area.

pts: Soil and moisture conservation: contour bunds, terraces, check dams, farm ponds, gully plugging; vegetative measures such as agroforestry and grass cover.
Water harvesting and groundwater recharge; community participation through user groups.
Integrated Watershed Management Programme under PMKSY (Watershed Development component), National Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Areas, Neeru-Chettu (AP) and MGNREGS works.
Rayalaseema's low and erratic rainfall, red and black soils prone to erosion, falling groundwater; watershed work and farm ponds improve drought-proofing.
Maintenance, equity in sharing benefits and weak convergence; need for scientific planning with remote sensing.

conclusion: Watershed management is the base of drought-proofing and sustainable farming. Community ownership keeps the structures working beyond project life.

theme: Human diseases: tuberculosis, malaria and HIV
question: Describe the causative agents, transmission, symptoms and preventive measures of tuberculosis and malaria. Mention the national programmes to control them.
why: Infectious diseases are asked 23 times, mostly as the 'agent, transmission, symptoms and control' form; TB, malaria, HIV and cholera are named in the syllabus.
intro: Tuberculosis and malaria are major infectious diseases of India. TB is caused by a bacterium and malaria by a protozoan parasite; both are preventable and curable.

pts: Agent: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; spread by droplets from pulmonary cases; symptoms: cough over two weeks, fever, weight loss, night sweats.
Diagnosis: sputum smear, CBNAAT/Truenat; treatment: DOTS with multi-drug regimen; MDR-TB and XDR-TB are concerns.
Prevention: BCG, early detection, nutrition (Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana), the National TB Elimination Programme with a goal of ending TB.
Agent: Plasmodium (P. vivax, P. falciparum), transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito; life cycle in mosquito and human liver and red blood cells; fever with chills, anaemia.
Prevention: bed nets, indoor spraying, larvicides, rapid tests and ACT drugs, vaccine R21 in some places; National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016–30).
Surveillance, early treatment, community participation (ASHA), sanitation and vector control, research and antimicrobial resistance monitoring.

conclusion: Both diseases can be controlled by early diagnosis, complete treatment and prevention at community level. Elimination needs sustained funding and attention to the poorest.
